title: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
summary: How map engines find the fastest route: road graphs from OpenStreetMap, Dijkstra, A* with admissible heuristics, contraction hierarchies, and real-world turn costs, traffic and time.
outcomes: Model a road network from OpenStreetMap as a directed graph with length or travel-time weights
Trace Dijkstra's algorithm with its priority queue and explain why a popped label is final
Explain why an admissible, consistent heuristic keeps A* optimal and settles fewer nodes
Contract nodes with witness searches and run an upward bidirectional contraction hierarchy query
Choose between CH and partition-based MLD given turn costs, traffic updates and time dependence

lessons.title: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph

blocks.md:
A routing engine answers questions like "what is the fastest way from here to there?" for any two points on a map, in milliseconds. To make that a computer problem, the road network becomes a **directed graph**: a set of **vertices** (junctions) and **arcs** (one-way road pieces between them). Each arc has a nonnegative **weight**, such as its length in meters or the time to drive it.

The **length of a path** is the sum of its arc weights, and the **point-to-point shortest path problem** asks for a path from a source $s$ to a target $t$ of minimum length, written $\mathrm{dist}(s,t)$.

blocks.title: From OpenStreetMap ways to graph edges

scenes.caption: Raw OSM: nodes are points with latitude and longitude; a way is an ordered list of nodes with tags. Way 1 is a two-way street, way 2 is tagged one-way from n6 to n3.
Simplify: n2 and n4 only shape the curve, so they are removed and their geometry is kept on the edge. Graph nodes remain only at junctions and dead ends.
Direct the edges: a two-way street becomes two reciprocal arcs, the one-way street a single arc. Each arc gets a weight such as length or travel time.

blocks.md: Tools such as [OSMnx](https://osmnx.readthedocs.io/en/stable/getting-started.html) automate this. OSMnx returns a NetworkX `MultiDiGraph`: a one-way street is a single directed edge from u to v, and a two-way street is two reciprocal edges. Its simplification step removes nodes that are not intersections or dead ends, and `add_edge_speeds` plus `add_edge_travel_times` turn lengths and (often imputed) speed limits into a `travel_time` weight in seconds.

Choose the weight to match the question. Minimizing `length` gives the shortest route in meters; minimizing `travel_time` gives the fastest. They often differ: a motorway detour can be longer but quicker.

For the rest of the course we use one tiny graph: 9 junctions and 14 two-way roads, with weights in minutes. S is the start, T the target. Every number in the figures was computed by a script running the algorithms on exactly this graph.

blocks.title: The toy road graph used in every lesson

scenes.caption: Nine junctions, fourteen two-way roads, weights in minutes. We route from S (west) to T (east). Grid cells are 1.25 km apart.
Fewest roads is not fastest: S, D, F, T (9 min), S, D, G, T (10 min) and S, C, F, T (14 min) all use 3 roads.
The fastest route is S, D, F, T at 9 minutes. Even this tiny graph has 22 simple S to T paths, from 9 to 28 minutes. Enumerating them does not scale.

blocks.md:
Two naive ideas fail. **Breadth-first search** finds the path with the fewest roads, but here three different 3-road routes take 9, 10 and 14 minutes, so hop count says nothing about time. **Trying every path** is hopeless: 22 simple paths already exist in 9 junctions, and the count grows exponentially with the size of the network.

Real inputs are huge. The standard research benchmark, the road network of Western Europe, has 18.0 million vertices and 42.5 million directed arcs.
A road network is a large, sparse, directed graph with **nonnegative** weights. Every fast routing algorithm in this course depends on the weights never being negative.

blocks.question: An OSM way is tagged `oneway=yes` and runs from node u to node v. How does it appear in a directed road graph such as an OSMnx MultiDiGraph?
options: As two arcs, u to v and v to u, with the second marked as forbidden
As an undirected edge with a flag that routing code checks
As a single arc from u to v
It is dropped, because one-way streets cannot be routed
blocks.explain: Direction is encoded in the graph itself: a one-way street contributes only the arc u to v, while a two-way street contributes two reciprocal arcs. The search then simply never finds a way to travel v to u on that street.

blocks.question: In the toy graph, a planner picks the route with the fewest roads and breaks ties arbitrarily. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing; fewest roads always means fastest when weights are minutes
It may return S, C, F, T (14 min) even though S, D, F, T takes 9 min
It cannot find any route, because BFS ignores weights entirely
It always returns the slowest 3-road route
blocks.explain: Three routes tie at 3 roads (9, 10 and 14 minutes). Hop count ignores weights, so any of them can come out. We need an algorithm that compares accumulated minutes, which is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm does.

lessons.title: Dijkstra's algorithm: settle nodes in order of distance

blocks.md:
Edsger W. Dijkstra published the classic solution in 1959 in a three-page note. The key fact: if R lies on a shortest path from P to Q, the part from P to R is itself a shortest path. So shortest paths can be built **in order of increasing length**, nearest node first, until the target is reached.

The note splits nodes into three sets: A, nodes whose minimum distance is known; B, nodes reachable from A but not yet final; C, the rest. Each step moves the node of B with the smallest distance into A and updates its neighbors.

blocks.caption: Relaxing the arc (u, v), where l(u, v) is its weight.

blocks.prompt: Our target T is 9 minutes from S. Before T is settled, how many of the other 8 junctions will Dijkstra settle?
blocks.reveal: **All 8.** Dijkstra settles nodes strictly in order of distance, and every other junction is closer than 9 minutes (A is 3, B is 4, E is 8). So it settles A and B, which lie behind S, before it ever settles T. The search is a ball around S, not a beam toward T.

blocks.title: Dijkstra's queue and labels, one pop per scene

scenes.caption: Start: S has tentative distance 0, every other node infinity. The queue holds only S.
Pop S (0) and settle it. Relax its four roads: A=3, B=4, D=2, C=7. Each becomes a queue entry.
Pop D (2), the smallest key. Relaxing D improves C from 7 to 6 (2+4) and reaches E=8, F=5, G=7.
Pop A (3). Its only other neighbor C already has 6, and 3+4=7 is worse, so nothing changes. A is settled although it lies behind S.
Pop B (4). Reaching E through B costs 4+5=9, worse than 8, so the queue is unchanged.
Pop F (5). Relaxing F reaches T for the first time: 5+4=9. T is in the queue but not settled yet.
Pop C (6). Every neighbor is already settled or has a better label.
Pop G (7). Going to T through G costs 7+3=10, worse than 9.
Pop E (8). Still not T: every node closer than 9 minutes must be settled first.
Pop T (9) and stop. All 9 nodes were settled to answer one query. Shortest route S, D, F, T in 9 minutes.

blocks.title: The settled set grows in every direction

scenes.caption: Settle S. Its neighbors A, B, C, D get tentative labels (badges); they form the frontier (blue).
Settle D at 2 minutes. C improves to 6 and the frontier spreads east to E, F and G.
A and B are settled next (3 and 4 minutes) although they lead away from T. Dijkstra knows nothing about direction.
F, C, G and E follow in distance order. The settled set is a growing ball around S.
T is settled last at 9 minutes, and the route is read back through parent pointers: S, D, F, T.

blocks.md: **Why the popped label is final.** When u has the smallest key in the queue, any other route to u must leave the settled set through some frontier node x with $d(x) \ge d(u)$, and the remaining arcs can only add nonnegative weight. So nothing can beat $d(u)$. That is why the search may **stop as soon as it pops t**, and why one negative weight breaks it.

blocks.caption: Dijkstra with a binary heap. Instead of decreasing keys, it pushes duplicates and skips stale entries; on the toy graph it returns 9 and settles 9 nodes.

blocks.md: With a binary heap the running time is $O((|V| + |A|)\log |V|)$. That is fast, but on Western Europe a random query still scans about 9.3 million vertices on average, roughly 2.2 seconds on the reference server of the Bast et al. survey. A web map needs answers thousands of times faster.

Common misconception: Dijkstra "heads toward" the target. It does not look at the target at all until it pops it. It settles every node closer than t, in all directions, which on a road map is a disc around s whose radius is the trip length.

blocks.question: A teammate stops Dijkstra as soon as T is first inserted into the queue, to save time. Using the toy run, why is this a bug in general?
options: It is not a bug; the first label any node receives is final
It only matters when the graph has negative weights
Insertion happens after settling, so the check never fires
Tentative labels can still drop after insertion, as C did (7 from S, then 6 via D)
blocks.explain: A label is only final when its node is popped as the queue minimum. C first got 7 directly from S and later improved to 6 through D. The same can happen to t, so the stop test must be on the pop, not the push.

blocks.question: Suppose one arc had weight -5 (say, a modeled time bonus). What breaks?
options: Correctness: a settled node's label might later be beaten through the negative arc
Only performance: the answer stays correct but slower
Nothing, as long as there is no negative cycle
The priority queue cannot store negative keys
blocks.explain: The finality argument assumes the rest of any path adds nonnegative length. A negative arc can make a path through a far node cheaper than an already settled label. Label-correcting methods such as Bellman-Ford handle negative weights, at higher cost.

lessons.title: A*: steering the search with a lower bound

blocks.md:
Hart, Nilsson and Raphael (1968) asked how knowledge about the problem can cut down the search while keeping the answer optimal. Their running example is exactly ours: the road distance between two cities can never be less than the straight-line (airline) distance between them.

**A*** is Dijkstra with a different queue key. Each node n gets an estimate $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$, where $g(n)$ is the best cost found so far from the start and $h(n)$ estimates the remaining cost to the goal.

blocks.tex: f(n) = g(n) + h(n), \qquad h(n) \le h^{*}(n)\ \text{for all } n
blocks.caption: h* is the true remaining cost. The paper proves (Theorem 1) that if h never overestimates it, A* is admissible: it always returns an optimal path.

blocks.md: For travel times we need a lower bound in **minutes**, so we divide straight-line distance by the fastest possible speed. In the toy, grid cells are 1.25 km apart and no road is faster than 60 km/h, so each straight-line kilometer is at least one minute: $h(S) = 5.0$, $h(D) = 3.75$, $h(A) = 6.73$. Every road weight in the graph is at least its straight-line length in minutes, so $h$ never overestimates.

The paper also states a **consistency assumption**, $h(m) \le \ell(m,n) + h(n)$ for every arc, a triangle inequality. Straight-line distance satisfies it, and then A* never has to reopen a closed node. An equivalent view: A* is Dijkstra on reduced weights $\ell(u,v) - h(u) + h(v)$, which consistency keeps nonnegative.

blocks.title: A* orders the queue by f = g + h

scenes.caption: Start: g(S)=0 and h(S)=5.0, so f(S)=5.0. The bottom row is the fixed heuristic: straight-line minutes to T.
Pop S. A, B, D, C enter with f = g + h. A has g=3 but f=9.7, because it lies 6.7 straight-line minutes from T.
Pop D (f 5.8). F gets f=6.8 and G gets 8.8, while C (10.5), E (12.5) and the westward nodes sink in the queue.
Pop F (f 6.8). T is reached with g=9, and h(T)=0, so f(T)=9.0.
Pop G (f 8.8). G is not on the best route, but its f is below 9, so the heuristic cannot rule it out yet.
Pop T (f 9.0) and stop. Only 5 nodes settled instead of 9. A, B, C and E stay in the queue unsettled.

blocks.prompt: G is not on the fastest route (S, D, F, T), yet A* settles it. Using the numbers in the last scenes, why?
blocks.reveal: A* must settle every node whose f is below the optimal cost. G has $g = 7$ and $h = 1.77$, so $f(G) \approx 8.8 < 9$. The straight line from G to T is short, but the road G to T takes 3 minutes, more than the bound promised. A tighter heuristic would skip G; a looser one would settle more.

blocks.title: A* settles a narrow band toward T

scenes.caption: Same graph, same query. Badges now show f = g + h for nodes in the queue.
After S and D: the eastward nodes F and G have the smallest f. A, B, C and E are reached but sit far back in the queue.
Settled set at the end: S, D, F, G, T. The westward nodes A and B were never settled because their f exceeds 9.

blocks.md: In practice the straight-line bound is weak on real road networks with travel times: it must divide by the top motorway speed, so it badly underestimates slow city streets. The Bast et al. survey reports the gain is small or nonexistent. **ALT** gets much better bounds from precomputed distances to a few landmarks plus the triangle inequality.

A* is Dijkstra with key g + h. Never overestimate (admissible) and you keep optimality; satisfy the triangle inequality (consistent) and each node is settled once. The closer h is to the true remaining cost, the fewer nodes settle.

blocks.question: What does A* do if h(n) = 0 for every node?
options: It settles exactly the nodes plain Dijkstra settles, since f = g
It fails, because 0 is not a valid lower bound
It settles only the nodes on the shortest path
It becomes breadth-first search
blocks.explain: Zero never overestimates, so it is admissible, but it gives no guidance: f equals g and the queue order is Dijkstra's. The paper notes this trivial estimate satisfies the consistency assumption.

blocks.question: To speed things up, someone divides straight-line km by 30 km/h instead of the network's top speed of 60 km/h. What is the risk?
options: None; any distance-based estimate keeps A* optimal
A* will settle more nodes than before
The heuristic may now overestimate on fast roads, so A* can return a slower route than the optimum
The algorithm may loop forever
blocks.explain: At 30 km/h each kilometer is estimated at 2 minutes, but a 60 km/h road covers it in 1. Overestimating breaks Theorem 1's condition, so optimality is no longer guaranteed. The survey notes such aggressive bounds speed things up only by giving up correctness.

blocks.md: **Bidirectional Dijkstra** runs two searches at once: forward from s, and backward from t over reversed arcs. It keeps $\mu$, the best $d_f(v) + d_b(v)$ seen at any node labeled by both. It can stop when the two queue minimums sum to at least $\mu$, since no undiscovered path can be shorter. On road networks it visits roughly half as many vertices.

blocks.title: Bidirectional Dijkstra meets in the middle

scenes.caption: Forward search settles S (green); backward search settles T (purple) on reversed arcs. Badges: f = forward label, b = backward label.
Forward settles D. F now has both labels, 5 forward and 4 backward, so a 9-minute route through F exists: best so far = 9.
Backward settles G (3). Its route through D would cost 2 + 8 = 10, no better than 9.
Forward settles A (3), backward settles F (4). Now the two queue minimums are 4 (B) and 6 (E): 4 + 6 = 10 is at least 9, so stop. 6 nodes settled, answer 9.

blocks.md:
Halving is not enough. **Contraction Hierarchies (CH)**, by Geisberger, Sanders, Schultes and Delling (WEA 2008), use **preprocessing**: work done once per map so that every later query is fast.

Fix an order of nodes by "importance". **Contract** them from least to most important: remove node v, and for each pair of its remaining neighbors u, w, add a **shortcut** arc (u, w) of weight $\ell(u,v) + \ell(v,w)$, but only if the path through v is the only shortest path from u to w.

blocks.caption: A path from u to w that avoids v and is no longer than the path through v is a witness; finding one means no shortcut is needed.

blocks.md: The check is a small Dijkstra search called a **witness search**. Real implementations limit it and may add a few unnecessary shortcuts, which is safe. The order matters a lot. The thesis behind the paper orders nodes with a priority queue whose main term is the **edge difference**: shortcuts added minus arcs removed when contracting v. The goal is a graph with as few arcs as possible.

blocks.title: Contracting F and G adds three shortcuts

scenes.caption: Node order chosen for this toy (least important first): F, G, A, B, C, E, S, T, D. We contract F first.
Contract F: for each pair of its neighbors, is the path through F the only shortest one? C to D via F costs 3 + 3 = 6, but the direct road C-D costs 4. That is a witness: no shortcut.
C to T via F costs 7 and the best path avoiding F costs 12; D to T via F costs 7 versus 8 avoiding F. No witness, so add shortcuts C-T (7) and D-T (7).
Contract G. D to T via G costs 8, but the new shortcut D-T (7) is a witness. E to T via G costs 6 versus 13 without G: add shortcut E-T (6).
The remaining contractions (A, B, C, E, S, T, then D) all find witnesses, so the hierarchy has exactly 3 shortcuts. D, ranked last, is the most important node.

blocks.md: **The query.** Run a bidirectional Dijkstra on the original graph plus shortcuts, but the forward search only follows arcs **to higher-ranked** nodes and the backward search only arcs **from higher-ranked** nodes. Geisberger et al. prove that both searches reach the highest-ranked node of a shortest path with exact labels, so the minimum $d_f(v) + d_b(v)$ over nodes reached by both is $\mathrm{dist}(s,t)$.

blocks.title: The CH query only climbs to higher ranks

scenes.caption: Query S to T on the graph plus shortcuts. From S the only arc to a higher rank goes to D (rank 9). From T the only one is the shortcut T-D (7).
Forward settles S and labels D = 2. Backward settles T and labels D = 7. D now has both labels: best so far 2 + 7 = 9.
Each side then settles D, which has no higher neighbor, so both queues empty and the search ends: 4 settle operations on 3 distinct nodes.
Unpack: the shortcut D-T (7) was created when F was contracted, so it stands for D, F, T (3 + 4). The final route is S, D, F, T in 9 minutes.

blocks.md: A CH query must not stop the first time the two searches meet. The meeting node with the best sum may be found later. Each side stops only when its own queue minimum is at least the best sum found so far.

blocks.title: Nodes settled for the S to T query

scenes.caption: Plain Dijkstra settles all 9 nodes because T is the farthest node from S.
Bidirectional Dijkstra settles 6 (3 per side). A* settles 5: the heuristic pushed A, B, C and E out.
The CH query does 4 settles on 3 distinct nodes, after paying for preprocessing once. On a continent the gap is far larger (next lesson).

blocks.md: CH trades a one-time preprocessing pass (contract nodes, add shortcuts) for tiny queries: two upward searches that meet at the most important node of the route, then shortcuts are unpacked back into original roads.

blocks.question: While contracting v, the path u, v, w costs 8, and a witness search finds a path from u to w avoiding v that also costs 8. What should the preprocessing do?
options: Add the shortcut, because ties must be preserved
Add the shortcut with weight 7 to prefer it
Abort the contraction of v
Skip the shortcut; an equally short path survives without v
blocks.explain: A shortcut is only needed when the path through v is the unique shortest path. An equally short witness keeps dist(u, w) correct in the remaining graph. In the toy, contracting G found a witness for D to T that is even shorter (the shortcut of weight 7 beats 8), so no shortcut was added there either.

blocks.question: After contraction, an important motorway is closed and its weight becomes very large. What happens to a plain CH built for the old weights?
options: Queries remain correct, since shortcuts are recomputed during each query
Shortcuts that include the motorway now carry stale weights, so the contraction (at least the weights) must be redone
Only the node order must change; shortcut weights update themselves
Nothing changes, because CH queries ignore original arc weights
blocks.explain: Shortcut weights are sums of original arc weights fixed at preprocessing time. The survey notes CH can keep its node order and rerun contraction for a new metric, but some recomputation is unavoidable. Handling frequent weight changes cheaply is what customizable methods target (next lesson).

lessons.title: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel

blocks.md: The Bast et al. survey (2015) compares speedup techniques on the Western Europe benchmark, with random source and target pairs on one core. Plain Dijkstra averages 2.2 s per query, bidirectional Dijkstra 1.2 s. CH needs 5 minutes of preprocessing and 0.4 GiB and then answers in 0.11 ms. The extremes show the trade space: Hub Labels answer in 0.56 microseconds but need 18.8 GiB.

blocks.title: Western Europe: vertices scanned per query (log10)

scenes.caption: Values are log10 of the average vertices scanned per random query on 18.0M vertices (Bast et al. survey, Table 1). Dijkstra: 9,326,696 (6.97).
Bidirectional search roughly halves the work: 4,914,804 (6.69). Still about 1.2 s per query on the survey's reference server.
With preprocessing: CRP (Customizable Route Planning, explained below) scans 2,766 vertices (1.65 ms) and CH scans 280 (0.11 ms). Each step down on this scale is a factor of 10.

blocks.md:
Those numbers use a **simplified model** that ignores turns. Real directions need **turn costs** (a left turn across traffic takes time) and **turn restrictions** (no left turn here, often an OSM relation). The survey describes two encodings:

- **arc-based** (edge-based): road segments become vertices and allowed turns become arcs, so the search remembers how it arrived;
- **compact**: keep intersections as vertices and attach turn tables to them.

OSRM's extractor builds an edge-expanded graph, and its Lua profile's `process_turn` function assigns a weight to every possible turn from its angle and road types.

blocks.prompt: In the toy, add a 4-minute penalty to the left turn S then D then F. Does the route still go through F?
blocks.reveal: No. S, D, F, T now costs 2 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 13 minutes, so the best route becomes S, D, G, T at 10 minutes. A node-based Dijkstra cannot see this: the cost of leaving D depends on which road you entered D from. The edge-based search tracks 28 directed road segments instead of 9 junctions.

blocks.title: A turn penalty changes the route

scenes.caption: Without turn costs the best route is S, D, F, T (9 minutes). Driving east into D, turning toward F (north) is a left turn.
Give the movement S then D then F a 4-minute penalty (waiting to cross oncoming traffic). That route now costs 13.
The best route becomes S, D, G, T (10 minutes). The search must now remember which road it arrived on, so it runs over the 28 directed road segments instead of the 9 junctions.

blocks.md: Turns hurt CH. In the survey's Table 2 (U-turns cost 100 s), CH on the compact turn model scans 1,998 vertices and takes 2.27 ms versus 280 and 0.11 ms without turns. **Customizable Route Planning (CRP)** stays near 1.7 ms with or without turns. CRP splits preprocessing into a slow metric-independent phase (a multilevel partition into cells) and a fast **customization** that recomputes shortcut weights between cell boundary vertices for a new metric, about 0.37 s on 12 cores.

[OSRM](https://github.com/Project-OSRM/osrm-backend) ships both families. **CH**: `osrm-contract` builds the hierarchy. **Multi-Level Dijkstra (MLD)**: `osrm-partition` splits the graph into a hierarchy of cells (default maximum cell sizes 128, 4096, 65536 and 2097152 nodes per level), and `osrm-customize` applies speed and turn-penalty files and can be rerun without re-partitioning when speeds change. The README recommends MLD by default and keeps CH for special cases such as very large distance matrices.

blocks.code:
# CH pipeline: one preprocessing step, rerun it to change weights
osrm-extract -p profiles/car.lua map.osm.pbf
osrm-contract map.osrm
osrm-routed --algorithm ch map.osrm

# MLD pipeline (recommended default): partition once,
# then re-customize whenever speeds change
osrm-extract -p profiles/car.lua map.osm.pbf
osrm-partition map.osrm
osrm-customize map.osrm --segment-speed-file speeds.csv
osrm-routed --algorithm mld map.osrm
blocks.caption: The two OSRM pipelines, after the OSRM docs. Both start from an OSM extract and a Lua profile; file names here are placeholders.

blocks.md: **Time-dependent routing.** Congestion repeats daily, so an arc can carry a **travel time function** of the departure time instead of one number. Dijkstra still works if leaving later never means arriving earlier, the **FIFO** (first in, first out) property. Bidirectional search gets harder, since the backward search does not know the arrival time, and shortcuts must store whole functions. Time-dependent variants of CH and ALT exist.

blocks.title: Rush hour on one road: does FIFO hold?

scenes.caption: Simplified model: travel time is 10 minutes plus a rush-hour bump peaking at 30 minutes for departures at 08:00. Arrival time only rises: leaving later never gets you there earlier (FIFO).
Make the jam clear up abruptly (width 10). Leaving at 65 arrives at 90.6, leaving at 70 arrives at 87.4: waiting would overtake. That breaks FIFO, which Dijkstra-style search relies on.
For this bump FIFO fails exactly when the arrival curve slopes down, here when width drops below about 17.2 minutes. Real speed profiles are built so arrival times never decrease.

blocks.md: No technique wins on every axis. Look at query time, preprocessing time, memory, how quickly new traffic weights can be applied, and whether turns and other metrics are supported. A static fastest-route server and a live-traffic service often choose differently.

Production routing = a graph from OSM (directed, with turn costs) + a preprocessing technique. CH gives the fastest queries on a fixed metric; partition-based MLD or CRP accepts new weights in seconds without redoing the expensive phase.

blocks.question: Your service ingests new traffic speeds every few minutes and must route with them right away. Which OSRM setup fits the docs' guidance?
options: MLD: partition once, rerun osrm-customize with the new speed file
CH, rerunning osrm-contract every few minutes
Plain Dijkstra with no preprocessing
CH with osrm-customize
blocks.explain: osrm-customize applies speed and turn-penalty files to a partitioned MLD graph and can be rerun without re-partitioning. CH's contraction would have to be redone, and osrm-customize is not part of the CH pipeline. Plain Dijkstra is far too slow at continental scale.

blocks.question: A travel time function says: leave at 08:05 and arrive at 08:30.6, or leave at 08:10 and arrive at 08:27.4. What does this violate, and why does it matter?
options: Admissibility; A* would overestimate
Nonnegative weights; travel times went negative
FIFO; waiting would beat leaving now, which breaks the label-setting search for earliest arrival
Turn restrictions; the profile is missing a penalty
blocks.explain: Leaving later and arriving earlier violates FIFO. Then arriving at a node as early as possible no longer guarantees arriving as early as possible further along, so a settled earliest-arrival label can be wrong. Dijkstra-style time-dependent search assumes FIFO, and the survey notes that other settings are studied separately.

blocks.question: Why does an edge-based (arc-based) graph make turn costs routable with an unchanged Dijkstra?
options: It deletes all intersections, so turns no longer exist
It stores turn costs in the heuristic
It merges parallel roads into one vertex
Its vertices are road segments, so a turn is an ordinary weighted arc between two segments
blocks.explain: Once a state is the road you are on, the cost of turning from it onto the next road is just an arc weight, and plain Dijkstra applies. The price is a larger graph: 28 directed segments instead of 9 junctions in the toy.
